author: basil

lemma.la: Ferunt enim, quod angelis dixerit: Faciamus hominem
lemma.en: For they say that he said it to the angels: let us make a human

original.text: Et dixit Deus, faciamus hominem. Ubi sunt nunc Judaei, qui in sequentibus velut per quasdam cavernas Deitatis luce fulgente, secundaque persona quae mystice quidem declaratur, necdum tamen manifeste conspicitur, repugnabant dicentes sibimet ipsum loqui Deum, quoniam ipse dixit et ipse fecit, Fiat lux, et facta est lux? Erant quidem in promptu, et nunc quae modo proferuntur ab eis ineptiae. Quis enim faber ferrarius, aut carpentarius, aut coriorum confector solus in suo consistens ergastulo, cui nullus artis socius praesto est, sibimet ipse dicit, faciamus gladium, vel aratrum compaginemus, aut formemus calceum; et non magis tacitus speciem quam mente destinavit inceptat? Etenim vana garrulitas est, hominum quempiam, velut judicem aut censorem districte sibimet aliquid imperare. Quanquam hi quoque qui Dominum crucifixerunt, quid non dicturi sint, exercitatas ad mendacium linguas habentes, licet praesens vox eorum penitus ora praecluserit? Et dixit Deus, Faciamus hominem. Donec igitur minime qui doceretur existeret, in profundo fuit abdita praedicatio Deitatis. Ubi vero coepit hominis exspectari creatio, revelata est fides, et evidenter dogma veritatis emicuit. Ausculta, Judaee Christi repugnator, quomodo socium mundificationis alloquitur, per quem saecula fecit, qui agit omnia verbo potentiae suae: sed tuus animus verba non recipit pietatis. Sicut enim ferae cum includuntur in caveis, vulvas earum dentibus exedunt, amaritudinem propriam demonstrantes, furorem tamen suum nequeunt explere: sic Judaeus adversarius veritatis, alligationum coarctatus angustiis, multas asserit esse personas ad quas Verbum Dei processisse mentitur. Ferunt enim, quod angelis dixerit: Faciamus hominem. Judaica vere fictio, suaeque digna perfidiae fabulositas! Ut unum non recipiant, plurimos confitentur, filiumque famulis per participationem dignitatis asciscunt, et conlibertos nostros auctores humanae formationis efficiunt, hominisque perfectorem volunt angelis coaequare, cum sit absurdum ut quaelibet factura possit aequalis esse factori. Consideremus quoque sequentia: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. Quid respondes? Nunquid Dei et angelorum una imago est? Nam Patris necesse est eamdem esse quam Filii, sic tamen, ut Deo decens intelligatur esse figura, id est, non in habitu corporeo, sed in divina proprietate consistens. Ausculta tu etiam, qui de nova circumcisione progrederis, Judaismi cultum sub Christianitatis simulatione commendans. Cui dicit, Ad imaginem nostram (Hebr. I, 3) , nisi illuminationi gloriae, et titulo paternae substantiae, quae est imago Dei invisibilis? Suae ergo loquitur imagini, quae dixit: Ego et Pater unum sumus (Joan. X, 30) ; et, Qui me videt et Patrem meum videt (Joan. XIV, 9) , huic dicit: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. Etenim ubi unitas imaginis est, nihil potest esse dissimile. Non enim dixit ad imagines nostras, sicut et Scriptura testatur: Fecit Deus, inquit, hominem: non fecerunt. Prudenter vitavit nunc multitudinem personarum: ut ubi quidem Judaeum confunderet, hic ritum gentilitatis excluderet. Ideo commemoravit unitatem, ut et Filium simul esse cum Patre cognosceres: et periculum de personarum multitudine declinares.

english.text: And God said, let us make a human. Where are the Jews now, who in what follows — where the light of the Godhead shines as if through certain caverns, and a second person is indeed declared mystically though not yet plainly seen — used to fight back, saying that God was speaking to himself, since he himself said and he himself made, 'let there be light', and there was light? Their absurdities were ready to hand then, as they are now brought out. For what blacksmith, or carpenter, or tanner of hides, standing alone in his workshop with no partner in the craft at hand, says to himself, let us make a sword, or let us put together a plough, or let us shape a shoe — and does not rather begin in silence upon the thing he has settled in his mind? It is empty chatter that any human being should sternly command something to himself, like a judge or a censor. Though what will these men not say, who crucified the Lord, having tongues trained to lying, even though the very voice now present has stopped their mouths altogether? And God said, let us make a human. So long, then, as there was no one to be taught, the preaching of the Godhead lay hidden in the deep. But when the creation of a human began to be looked for, faith was revealed, and the teaching of the truth plainly flashed out. Listen, Jew, you fighter against Christ, how he addresses the partner of the world's making, through whom he made the ages, who does all things by the word of his power: but your mind does not receive the words of piety. For as wild beasts, when they are shut in cages, gnaw at their own wombs with their teeth, showing their own bitterness and yet unable to work off their fury, so the Jew, the adversary of the truth, hemmed in by the straits of these bindings, asserts that there are many persons to whom the Word of God went out, and lies in saying it. For they say that he said it to the angels: let us make a human. A Jewish fiction, truly, and a fabling worthy of their perfidy! So as not to receive one, they confess many; they take the Son into fellowship with servants by a sharing of dignity, and make our fellow slaves the authors of the human form, and want the one who perfected the human to be equalled with angels — when it is absurd that any thing made should be equal to its maker. Let us consider what follows too: let us make a human to our image. What do you answer? Is there one image of God and of the angels? For the Father's must necessarily be the same as the Son's, yet in such a way that the figure is understood as befits God, that is, not consisting in bodily form but in the divine property. Listen, you too, who come forward out of the new circumcision, commending the cult of Judaism under a pretence of Christianity. To whom does he say, to our image, if not to the radiance of the glory and the stamp of the paternal substance, which is the image of the invisible God? He speaks, then, to his own image, which said: I and the Father are one; and, whoever sees me sees my Father also — to this one he says: let us make a human to our image. For where there is a unity of image, nothing can be unlike. For he did not say, to our images, as Scripture also testifies: God made, it says, the human: they did not make. He prudently avoided a multitude of persons here: so that where he confounded the Jew, here he might shut out the rite of the gentiles. Therefore he called to mind the unity, so that you might know the Son to be together with the Father, and might avoid the danger of a multitude of persons.

notes: ⚠ Anchor note: this is a comment on Gen 1:26, not on Gen 1:1–5. It is on the daf under the second clause of the anchor rule — it argues the same philological question the Elohim of Gen 1:1 raises, whether a plural form of speech about God implies a plurality in God — and is anchored on Gen 1:2 beside that material. The most violent page on the site, and the one that proves the two benches were in contact on this question, because it is an answer to an argument the rabbinic bench is on record making. Basil — in Eustathius's Latin, which is how the Latin bench read him — knows three Jewish readings of the plural and takes them in order: that God spoke to himself, which he answers with the workshop analogy (no smith alone says 'let us make a sword'); that God spoke to the angels, which he calls a Jewish fiction and answers from the image (there is not one image of God and of the angels); and, underneath both, that the plural cannot mean persons. Then the sentence that matters most for this daf: Fecit Deus, inquit, hominem: non fecerunt — 'God made the human: they did not make'. That is the singular-verb argument of Bereshit Rabbah 1:7 and of R. Simlai at Bereshit Rabbah 8:9, in Latin, used to the opposite end. The abuse is not incidental and is not softened here: the Jew is a beast gnawing its own womb, the reading is perfidia, and the passage ends by turning on judaizing Christians. It is also, and this is the point for the finding, a Christian text that knows what the other bench says and answers it by name.
